newsitem.title: FRANCE: Spanish Civil War veterans attend Paris ceremony.
newsitem.headline: Spanish Civil War veterans attend Paris ceremony.

text.p: Veterans of the Spanish Civil War marked the 60th anniversary of the creation of the International Brigades on Saturday and warned of future civil strife in France if rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen was not stopped.

"In Spain, the cry was "no pasaran" (they shall not pass). Here, the cry must be "No, No, fascism will not be allowed to pass," said veteran Louis Blesy in an impassioned speech to several hundred people in the Paris suburb of Montreuil, a traditional working class bastion.

Blesy, now in his 80s, was a metalworker who became an officer in the International Brigades fighting to defend the Spanish Republic against insurgent General Francisco Franco in the 1936-1939 Spanish Civil War.
Blesy, who later played a key role in the World War Two French Resistance, likened the current rise of Le Pen's National Front (NF) party to that of fascist movements in France before World War Two.

"The exaggerated nationalism, the creeping racism, it's all the same, it's the return of Vichy (the wartime French collaborationist regime). Like then, we must be ready to face the danger and take action if Le Pen is not stopped before," Blesy said.

He spoke at the unveiling of a small monument on a windswept square in memory of the estimated 35,000 men and women from 53 countries who formed the International Brigades, suffered 10,000 dead and earned a place in the pantheon of left-wing heroes.
While half the volunteers were non-communists, the Brigades' leadership was overwhelmingly communist.
The Brigades were created in October 1936, three months after the start of the civil war and Montreuil was an assembly point for volunteers and supplies from France.
The French were the single largest national contingent in the Brigades, supplying 9,000 volunteers of whom about a third were killed.
Their senior surviving officer, retired Colonel Henri Rol-Tanguy told reporters that a gathering of survivors still alive from around the world was planned for the months ahead in Madrid.

The square where the monument was unveiled was itself renamed "Esplanade Guernica" in honour of a Spanish Basque town whose bombing by rebel aircraft inspired one of painter Pablo Picasso's best-known works.
Guernica's current mayor, Eduardo Vallejo de Olejua, and Spanish diplomats were present at the Montreuil ceremony.
